content:
This page takes you from an empty project to a passing permission check, then layers on ABAC policies, owner-only conditions, multi-tenant scopes, server guards, and a client permission map. Every snippet is checked against the current `@gentleduck/iam`. If you only have five minutes, stop after step 4 - that is the first passing check. ## The path Steps 1 to 4 are the vertical slice: a subject with a role, a grant, and a decision. Steps 5 to 9 are layers you add when you need them - attribute rules, ownership, tenancy, then moving the decision out to your routes and your UI. S2["2. createIam(): declare actions, resources, roles"] S2 --> S3["3. defineRole(): grant action x resource pairs"] S3 --> S4["4. IamMemoryAdapter + createEngine() -> engine.can()"] S4 --> S5["5. definePolicy(): ABAC rules and conditions"] S4 --> S6["6. grantWhen(): owner-only permissions"] S4 --> S7["7. Scoped roles for multi-tenancy"] S4 --> S8["8. Server guard on a route"] S8 --> S9["9. engine.permissions() -> client permission map"]`} /> ## Step 1: install The package has one runtime dependency (`uuid`, pulled in only by the Drizzle schema helpers). Every adapter, server middleware, and client library lives behind a subpath export, so you only bundle what you import. ## Step 2: declare your access config `createIam()` is the entry point. Pass your actions and resources as `as const` arrays; the returned config threads those literal unions through every builder. ```ts title="src/lib/access.ts" import { createIam } from '@gentleduck/iam/core' export const access = createIam({ actions: ['create', 'read', 'update', 'delete', 'manage'] as const, resources: ['post', 'comment', 'user', 'team', 'billing'] as const, roles: ['viewer', 'editor', 'moderator', 'admin', 'author'] as const, scopes: ['org-1', 'org-2'] as const, }) ``` `as const` is what makes the config type-safe. Without it TypeScript infers `string[]` and every builder falls back to accepting any string. With it, `access.defineRole('viewer').grant('craete', 'post')` is a compile error because `'craete'` is not in the actions tuple. | Option | Type | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `actions` | `readonly string[]` | required | Actions your application supports | | `resources` | `readonly string[]` | required | Resource types your application manages | | `roles` | `readonly string[]` | `[]` | Role IDs; constrains `defineRole` and `assignRole` | | `scopes` | `readonly string[]` | `[]` | Scope strings for multi-tenant authorization | | `context` | `object` | `DotPath.IDefaultContext` | Phantom field for typed dot-paths. Pass `{} as unknown as AppContext`; the runtime value is never read | The returned object exposes `defineRole`, `definePolicy`, `defineRule`, `when`, `createEngine`, `checks`, `validateRoles`, and `validatePolicy`. Full reference: [createIam options](/duck-iam/advanced/config/access-config). ## Step 3: define roles Roles are collections of `(action, resource)` grants. `inherits` closes over parent roles at load time. ```ts title="src/lib/roles.ts" import { access } from './access' export const viewer = access .defineRole('viewer') .desc('Read-only access to content') .grantRead('post', 'comment') .build() export const editor = access .defineRole('editor') .desc('Can create and edit content') .inherits('viewer') .grant('create', 'post') .grant('update', 'post') .grant('create', 'comment') .grant('update', 'comment') .build() export const moderator = access .defineRole('moderator') .desc('Can delete content') .inherits('editor') .grant('delete', 'post') .grant('delete', 'comment') .build() export const admin = access .defineRole('admin') .desc('Full access') .inherits('moderator') .grantCRUD('user') .grant('manage', 'team') .grant('manage', 'billing') .build() export const allRoles = [viewer, editor, moderator, admin] ``` `grantRead(...resources)` is shorthand for `grant('read', r)` per resource. `grantCRUD(resource)` expands to `create`, `read`, `update`, `delete`. `grantAll(resource)` grants `'*'` on that resource. `build()` runs the validator and throws if the role is malformed - a dangling `inherits`, an empty role, an inheritance chain deeper than the runtime's `MAX_INHERITANCE_DEPTH` of 32. It throws `IAM_VALIDATION_FAILED` (`meta: { kind: 'role', issues: string[] }`), the same coded error `PolicyBuilder.build()` throws. See [role definition](/duck-iam/core/roles/definition) and [inheritance](/duck-iam/core/roles/inheritance). `inherits` is additive only. To restrict access below what a parent grants, add an ABAC deny policy - see [combining algorithms](/duck-iam/core/policies/combining-algorithms). ## Step 4: create the engine and run your first check ```ts title="src/lib/engine.ts" import { IamMemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/iam/adapters/memory' import { access } from './access' import { allRoles } from './roles' const adapter = new IamMemoryAdapter({ roles: allRoles, assignments: { 'user-alice': ['admin'], 'user-bob': ['editor'], 'user-carol': ['viewer'], }, }) export const engine = access.createEngine({ adapter }) ``` ```ts // Alice is an admin - she can do everything. await engine.can('user-alice', 'manage', { type: 'billing', attributes: {} }) // -> true // Bob is an editor - he can create posts but not delete them. await engine.can('user-bob', 'create', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> true await engine.can('user-bob', 'delete', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> false // Carol is a viewer - reads only. await engine.can('user-carol', 'read', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> true await engine.can('user-carol', 'create', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> false ``` That is the first passing check. `can(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` always returns a plain `boolean`, in either engine mode, and never rejects - a subject-resolution failure or an adapter timeout is routed to `hooks.onError` and returns `false`. ### What the engine did Here is the path that first `can()` call took. >E: "can('user-bob', 'create', post)" E->>SC: "get('user-bob')" SC-->>E: "miss" E->>A: "getSubjectRoles + getSubjectAttributes + listRoles" A-->>E: "['editor'] and attributes" E->>E: "resolve inherits -> ['editor','viewer']" E->>SC: "set('user-bob', subject)" E->>A: "listPolicies" A-->>E: "[] plus generated RBAC policy" E->>Ev: "evaluate(policies, request)" Ev-->>E: "IDecision allowed=true" E-->>App: "true"`} /> The subject cache miss is what makes the first call expensive; every later call for `user-bob` inside the TTL window skips the adapter entirely. `listRoles` is fetched because inheritance is flattened at load, not per request. The roles are compiled into an ABAC policy by `rolesToPolicy()`, so an RBAC grant and an attribute policy go through the same evaluator - there is no second code path. See [evaluation pipeline](/duck-iam/core/evaluation) and [caching](/duck-iam/advanced/engine/caching). ### `can` vs `check` vs `authorize` vs `explain` | Method | Input | Returns | |---|---|---| | `can(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` | subject ID | `Promise` always | | `check(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` | subject ID | `Promise` in production mode, `Promise` in development | | `authorize(request)` | a full `IamRequest.IAccessRequest` you built yourself | mode-dependent, same as `check` | | `explain(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` | subject ID | `Promise`; throws in production mode | | `permissions(subjectId, checks, environment?, opts?)` | subject ID plus up to 1024 checks | a permission map | Full signatures: [engine methods](/duck-iam/advanced/engine/methods). ## Step 5: add an ABAC policy Roles answer "who". Policies answer "under what conditions". This one blocks writes outside business hours. ```ts title="src/lib/policies.ts" import { access } from './access' export const businessHoursPolicy = access .definePolicy('business-hours') .name('Business hours only') .desc('Deny write operations outside 09:00-18:00 UTC') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .rule('deny-after-hours', (r) => r .deny() .on('create', 'update', 'delete') .of('post', 'comment') .whenAny((w) => w.env('hour', 'lt', 9).env('hour', 'gte', 18)) .desc('Block writes outside business hours'), ) .build() ``` ```ts await engine.admin.savePolicy(businessHoursPolicy) await engine.can( 'user-bob', 'create', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }, { hour: 22 }, ) // -> false ``` `whenAny` is OR: the rule fires when the hour is before 9 **or** at 18 and later. `env('hour', ...)` is shorthand for the dot-path `environment.hour`, read from the `environment` object, the fourth argument to `can()`. `algorithm('deny-overrides')` is the default and means any deny inside this policy wins. The four intra-policy combining algorithms are `deny-overrides` (default), `allow-overrides`, `first-match`, and `highest-priority`. Across policies the engine's `policyCombine` setting applies - `'and'` by default, meaning every applicable policy must allow. See [combining algorithms](/duck-iam/core/policies/combining-algorithms) and [cross-policy combination](/duck-iam/core/cross-policy). `.target({ actions, resources })` skips the policy when the request does not match. If the target admits a pair that none of the policy's allow rules covers, `build()` throws `UNREACHABLE_TARGET` - every request matching that target would be denied silently. Add a rule that allows the pair, or narrow the target. See [targets](/duck-iam/core/policies/targets). ## Step 6: owner-only permissions `grantWhen` attaches a condition to a single grant. `w.isOwner()` is shorthand for `resource.attributes.ownerId eq $subject.id`. ```ts title="src/lib/roles.ts" export const author = access .defineRole('author') .desc('Can update and delete own posts only') .inherits('viewer') .grant('create', 'post') .grantWhen('update', 'post', (w) => w.isOwner()) .grantWhen('delete', 'post', (w) => w.isOwner()) .build() ``` Pass the resource's attributes on the check so the condition has something to read: ```ts await engine.admin.saveRole(author) await engine.admin.assignRole('user-dana', 'author') await engine.can('user-dana', 'update', { type: 'post', id: 'post-123', attributes: { ownerId: 'user-dana' }, }) // -> true await engine.can('user-dana', 'update', { type: 'post', id: 'post-123', attributes: { ownerId: 'user-alice' }, }) // -> false ``` The `$` prefix marks a value as a reference into the request rather than a literal. At evaluation time `$subject.id` resolves against the request that is being evaluated. Pass a different owner field with `w.isOwner('resource.attributes.createdBy')`. See [dollar variables](/duck-iam/core/policies/dollar-variables). `eq` is `===`. A subject ID of `'42'` never equals an `ownerId` of `42`. `gt` / `gte` / `lt` / `lte` return `false` unless **both** operands are numbers, so an ISO date string compared with `gte` is always false - use `before` / `after` for temporal values. ## Step 7: multi-tenant scoped roles Assign the same subject different roles per scope, then pass the scope on the check. ```ts // Alice is admin in org-1 but only a viewer in org-2. await engine.admin.assignRole('user-alice', 'admin', 'org-1') await engine.admin.assignRole('user-alice', 'viewer', 'org-2') await engine.can('user-alice', 'manage', { type: 'team', attributes: {} }, undefined, 'org-1') // -> true await engine.can('user-alice', 'manage', { type: 'team', attributes: {} }, undefined, 'org-2') // -> false ``` The engine merges the subject's global roles with the scoped assignments whose scope matches the request. Matching is exact by default (`scopeMode: 'flat'`). Set `scopeMode: 'hierarchical'` on the engine config to treat a dot-delimited scope as a path, so a grant on `'org-1'` applies to `'org-1.team-2.repo-3'`. See [scoped roles](/duck-iam/core/roles/scoped). `engine.getEffectiveRoles(subjectId, scope?)` returns the merged list if you need to see what the engine resolved. ## Step 8: guard a route Every framework wrapper is built on `engine.can()` and takes the same three leading arguments. ### Express ```ts title="src/server.ts" import express from 'express' import { iamAccessMiddleware, iamGuard } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/express' import { engine } from './lib/engine' const app = express() // Option A: global middleware, infers action from the HTTP method and // resource from the first path segment. app.use(iamAccessMiddleware(engine, { getUserId: (req) => req.user?.id ?? null })) // Option B: an explicit per-route guard. app.get('/posts', iamGuard(engine, 'read', 'post'), (req, res) => res.json({ posts: [] })) app.delete('/posts/:id', iamGuard(engine, 'delete', 'post'), (req, res) => res.json({ deleted: true })) app.listen(3000) ``` `iamGuard` reads the resource ID from `req.params.id`. Both helpers reply 401 when `getUserId` returns null and 403 when the engine denies. ### Hono ```ts title="src/worker.ts" import { Hono } from 'hono' import { iamAccessMiddleware, iamGuard } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/hono' import { engine } from './lib/engine' const app = new Hono() app.use('*', iamAccessMiddleware(engine, { getUserId: (c) => (c.get('userId') as string | null) ?? null })) app.delete('/posts/:id', iamGuard(engine, 'delete', 'post'), (c) => c.json({ deleted: true })) export default app ``` ### NestJS ```ts title="src/posts/posts.controller.ts" import { Controller, Delete, Get, Param, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common' import { IamAuthorize, iamNestAccessGuard } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/nest' import { engine } from '../lib/engine' const canActivate = iamNestAccessGuard(engine, { getUserId: (req) => req.user?.sub ?? null }) @Controller('posts') @UseGuards({ canActivate } as never) export class PostsController { @Get() @IamAuthorize({ action: 'read', resource: 'post' }) findAll() { return [] } @Delete(':id') @IamAuthorize({ action: 'delete', resource: 'post' }) remove(@Param('id') id: string) { return { deleted: id } } } ``` `iamNestAccessGuard` returns a `canActivate` body; handlers with no `IamAuthorize` metadata pass through. ### Next.js ```ts title="src/app/api/posts/[id]/route.ts" import { withIamAccess } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/next' import { engine } from '@/lib/engine' import { getSession } from '@/lib/auth' export const DELETE = withIamAccess( engine, 'delete', 'post', async (req, ctx) => { const params = ctx.params instanceof Promise ? await ctx.params : ctx.params return Response.json({ deleted: params?.id }) }, { getUserId: async () => { const session = await getSession() return session?.userId ?? null }, }, ) ``` Since 2.1.0 `withIamAccess` throws at construction when `getUserId` is omitted, and the Hono helpers read only `c.get('userId')` - there is no `x-user-id` header fallback on any framework. A raw request header is spoofable with one `curl`. Derive identity from a cookie session, a JWT your middleware verified, or mTLS. See [production hardening](/duck-iam/guides/production). Per-framework detail: [express](/duck-iam/integrations/server/express), [hono](/duck-iam/integrations/server/hono), [nest](/duck-iam/integrations/server/nest), [next](/duck-iam/integrations/server/next). ## Step 9: send a permission map to the client `engine.permissions()` evaluates a batch of checks in one pass and returns a map keyed by `iamBuildPermissionKey`: `action:resource[:resourceId]`, or `@scope:action:resource[:resourceId]` when a scope is passed - the leading `@` is what keeps a scoped key unambiguous, so it is never dropped. Serialize it into your page and the client checks become synchronous object lookups. ```tsx title="src/app/layout.tsx" import { getIamPermissions } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/next' import { engine } from '@/lib/engine' import { getSession } from '@/lib/auth' import { AccessProvider } from '@/lib/access-client' export default async function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const session = await getSession() const permissions = await getIamPermissions(engine, session.userId, [ { action: 'create', resource: 'post' }, { action: 'delete', resource: 'post' }, { action: 'manage', resource: 'team' }, ]) return {children} } ``` ```ts title="src/lib/access-client.tsx" 'use client' import React from 'react' import { createIamAccessControl } from '@gentleduck/iam/client/react' export const { AccessProvider, useAccess, usePermissions, Can, Cannot } = createIamAccessControl(React) ``` ```tsx title="src/components/post-actions.tsx" 'use client' import { Can, Cannot, useAccess } from '@/lib/access-client' export function PostActions() { const { can } = useAccess() return (
{can('update', 'post') && }

You do not have permission to manage this team.
) } ``` `createIamAccessControl(React)` takes the host React module as an argument so the package never bundles its own copy. `permissions()` refuses batches over 1024 checks - that is a caller bug, and it throws rather than failing closed. See [permission map](/duck-iam/integrations/client/permission-map) and [React client](/duck-iam/integrations/client/react). ## Debugging with explain When a decision surprises you, `engine.explain()` returns the whole trace. It is development-mode only and throws the coded `IAM_ENGINE_EXPLAIN_UNAVAILABLE` otherwise. ```ts const trace = await engine.explain('user-dana', 'delete', { type: 'post', id: 'post-123', attributes: { ownerId: 'user-alice' }, }) trace.decision // AccessControl.IDecision: { allowed, effect, reason, duration, timestamp, ... } trace.summary // human-readable one-liner trace.subject // { id, roles, scopedRolesApplied, attributes } trace.policies // Explain.IPolicyTrace[]: per policy, per rule, per condition, // with actual vs expected for every comparison ``` `explain()` does not fire `afterEvaluate`, `onDeny`, or `onError` - it is read-only. It does run `beforeEvaluate`, because that hook changes what is evaluated. Field-by-field reference: [explain](/duck-iam/advanced/explain). ## Before you ship The engine defaults to `mode: 'development'`, which allocates a full `IDecision` per policy per request. Production deployments should set `mode: 'production'`, call `engine.preload()` at boot, and `engine.dispose()` on shutdown. Work through the [production hardening checklist](/duck-iam/guides/production) before you take traffic. ## See also * [Production hardening](/duck-iam/guides/production) - the pre-flight checklist, with a link per item * [Cookbook](/duck-iam/guides/cookbook) - recipes for the patterns above ownership and tenancy * [Troubleshooting](/duck-iam/guides/troubleshooting) - symptom, cause, fix, keyed to real error messages * [Core concepts](/duck-iam/core) - policies, rules, conditions, combining algorithms * [Pairing with duck-auth](/duck-iam/guides/auth-bridge) - where the subject ID comes from * [Real-world examples](/duck-iam/guides/examples) - this walkthrough's patterns, wired into four real framework backends

This page takes you from an empty project to a passing permission check, then layers on ABAC policies, owner-only conditions, multi-tenant scopes, server guards, and a client permission map. Every snippet is checked against the current `@gentleduck/iam`. If you only have five minutes, stop after step 4 - that is the first passing check. ## The path Steps 1 to 4 are the vertical slice: a subject with a role, a grant, and a decision. Steps 5 to 9 are layers you add when you need them - attribute rules, ownership, tenancy, then moving the decision out to your routes and your UI. S2["2. createIam(): declare actions, resources, roles"] S2 --> S3["3. defineRole(): grant action x resource pairs"] S3 --> S4["4. IamMemoryAdapter + createEngine() -> engine.can()"] S4 --> S5["5. definePolicy(): ABAC rules and conditions"] S4 --> S6["6. grantWhen(): owner-only permissions"] S4 --> S7["7. Scoped roles for multi-tenancy"] S4 --> S8["8. Server guard on a route"] S8 --> S9["9. engine.permissions() -> client permission map"]`} /> ## Step 1: install The package has one runtime dependency (`uuid`, pulled in only by the Drizzle schema helpers). Every adapter, server middleware, and client library lives behind a subpath export, so you only bundle what you import. ## Step 2: declare your access config `createIam()` is the entry point. Pass your actions and resources as `as const` arrays; the returned config threads those literal unions through every builder. ```ts title="src/lib/access.ts" import { createIam } from '@gentleduck/iam/core' export const access = createIam({ actions: ['create', 'read', 'update', 'delete', 'manage'] as const, resources: ['post', 'comment', 'user', 'team', 'billing'] as const, roles: ['viewer', 'editor', 'moderator', 'admin', 'author'] as const, scopes: ['org-1', 'org-2'] as const, }) ``` `as const` is what makes the config type-safe. Without it TypeScript infers `string[]` and every builder falls back to accepting any string. With it, `access.defineRole('viewer').grant('craete', 'post')` is a compile error because `'craete'` is not in the actions tuple. | Option | Type | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `actions` | `readonly string[]` | required | Actions your application supports | | `resources` | `readonly string[]` | required | Resource types your application manages | | `roles` | `readonly string[]` | `[]` | Role IDs; constrains `defineRole` and `assignRole` | | `scopes` | `readonly string[]` | `[]` | Scope strings for multi-tenant authorization | | `context` | `object` | `DotPath.IDefaultContext` | Phantom field for typed dot-paths. Pass `{} as unknown as AppContext`; the runtime value is never read | The returned object exposes `defineRole`, `definePolicy`, `defineRule`, `when`, `createEngine`, `checks`, `validateRoles`, and `validatePolicy`. Full reference: [createIam options](/duck-iam/advanced/config/access-config). ## Step 3: define roles Roles are collections of `(action, resource)` grants. `inherits` closes over parent roles at load time. ```ts title="src/lib/roles.ts" import { access } from './access' export const viewer = access .defineRole('viewer') .desc('Read-only access to content') .grantRead('post', 'comment') .build() export const editor = access .defineRole('editor') .desc('Can create and edit content') .inherits('viewer') .grant('create', 'post') .grant('update', 'post') .grant('create', 'comment') .grant('update', 'comment') .build() export const moderator = access .defineRole('moderator') .desc('Can delete content') .inherits('editor') .grant('delete', 'post') .grant('delete', 'comment') .build() export const admin = access .defineRole('admin') .desc('Full access') .inherits('moderator') .grantCRUD('user') .grant('manage', 'team') .grant('manage', 'billing') .build() export const allRoles = [viewer, editor, moderator, admin] ``` `grantRead(...resources)` is shorthand for `grant('read', r)` per resource. `grantCRUD(resource)` expands to `create`, `read`, `update`, `delete`. `grantAll(resource)` grants `'*'` on that resource. `build()` runs the validator and throws if the role is malformed - a dangling `inherits`, an empty role, an inheritance chain deeper than the runtime's `MAX_INHERITANCE_DEPTH` of 32. It throws `IAM_VALIDATION_FAILED` (`meta: { kind: 'role', issues: string[] }`), the same coded error `PolicyBuilder.build()` throws. See [role definition](/duck-iam/core/roles/definition) and [inheritance](/duck-iam/core/roles/inheritance). `inherits` is additive only. To restrict access below what a parent grants, add an ABAC deny policy - see [combining algorithms](/duck-iam/core/policies/combining-algorithms). ## Step 4: create the engine and run your first check ```ts title="src/lib/engine.ts" import { IamMemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/iam/adapters/memory' import { access } from './access' import { allRoles } from './roles' const adapter = new IamMemoryAdapter({ roles: allRoles, assignments: { 'user-alice': ['admin'], 'user-bob': ['editor'], 'user-carol': ['viewer'], }, }) export const engine = access.createEngine({ adapter }) ``` ```ts // Alice is an admin - she can do everything. await engine.can('user-alice', 'manage', { type: 'billing', attributes: {} }) // -> true // Bob is an editor - he can create posts but not delete them. await engine.can('user-bob', 'create', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> true await engine.can('user-bob', 'delete', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> false // Carol is a viewer - reads only. await engine.can('user-carol', 'read', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> true await engine.can('user-carol', 'create', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }) // -> false ``` That is the first passing check. `can(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` always returns a plain `boolean`, in either engine mode, and never rejects - a subject-resolution failure or an adapter timeout is routed to `hooks.onError` and returns `false`. ### What the engine did Here is the path that first `can()` call took. >E: "can('user-bob', 'create', post)" E->>SC: "get('user-bob')" SC-->>E: "miss" E->>A: "getSubjectRoles + getSubjectAttributes + listRoles" A-->>E: "['editor'] and attributes" E->>E: "resolve inherits -> ['editor','viewer']" E->>SC: "set('user-bob', subject)" E->>A: "listPolicies" A-->>E: "[] plus generated RBAC policy" E->>Ev: "evaluate(policies, request)" Ev-->>E: "IDecision allowed=true" E-->>App: "true"`} /> The subject cache miss is what makes the first call expensive; every later call for `user-bob` inside the TTL window skips the adapter entirely. `listRoles` is fetched because inheritance is flattened at load, not per request. The roles are compiled into an ABAC policy by `rolesToPolicy()`, so an RBAC grant and an attribute policy go through the same evaluator - there is no second code path. See [evaluation pipeline](/duck-iam/core/evaluation) and [caching](/duck-iam/advanced/engine/caching). ### `can` vs `check` vs `authorize` vs `explain` | Method | Input | Returns | |---|---|---| | `can(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` | subject ID | `Promise` always | | `check(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` | subject ID | `Promise` in production mode, `Promise` in development | | `authorize(request)` | a full `IamRequest.IAccessRequest` you built yourself | mode-dependent, same as `check` | | `explain(subjectId, action, resource, environment?, scope?)` | subject ID | `Promise`; throws in production mode | | `permissions(subjectId, checks, environment?, opts?)` | subject ID plus up to 1024 checks | a permission map | Full signatures: [engine methods](/duck-iam/advanced/engine/methods). ## Step 5: add an ABAC policy Roles answer "who". Policies answer "under what conditions". This one blocks writes outside business hours. ```ts title="src/lib/policies.ts" import { access } from './access' export const businessHoursPolicy = access .definePolicy('business-hours') .name('Business hours only') .desc('Deny write operations outside 09:00-18:00 UTC') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .rule('deny-after-hours', (r) => r .deny() .on('create', 'update', 'delete') .of('post', 'comment') .whenAny((w) => w.env('hour', 'lt', 9).env('hour', 'gte', 18)) .desc('Block writes outside business hours'), ) .build() ``` ```ts await engine.admin.savePolicy(businessHoursPolicy) await engine.can( 'user-bob', 'create', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }, { hour: 22 }, ) // -> false ``` `whenAny` is OR: the rule fires when the hour is before 9 **or** at 18 and later. `env('hour', ...)` is shorthand for the dot-path `environment.hour`, read from the `environment` object, the fourth argument to `can()`. `algorithm('deny-overrides')` is the default and means any deny inside this policy wins. The four intra-policy combining algorithms are `deny-overrides` (default), `allow-overrides`, `first-match`, and `highest-priority`. Across policies the engine's `policyCombine` setting applies - `'and'` by default, meaning every applicable policy must allow. See [combining algorithms](/duck-iam/core/policies/combining-algorithms) and [cross-policy combination](/duck-iam/core/cross-policy). `.target({ actions, resources })` skips the policy when the request does not match. If the target admits a pair that none of the policy's allow rules covers, `build()` throws `UNREACHABLE_TARGET` - every request matching that target would be denied silently. Add a rule that allows the pair, or narrow the target. See [targets](/duck-iam/core/policies/targets). ## Step 6: owner-only permissions `grantWhen` attaches a condition to a single grant. `w.isOwner()` is shorthand for `resource.attributes.ownerId eq $subject.id`. ```ts title="src/lib/roles.ts" export const author = access .defineRole('author') .desc('Can update and delete own posts only') .inherits('viewer') .grant('create', 'post') .grantWhen('update', 'post', (w) => w.isOwner()) .grantWhen('delete', 'post', (w) => w.isOwner()) .build() ``` Pass the resource's attributes on the check so the condition has something to read: ```ts await engine.admin.saveRole(author) await engine.admin.assignRole('user-dana', 'author') await engine.can('user-dana', 'update', { type: 'post', id: 'post-123', attributes: { ownerId: 'user-dana' }, }) // -> true await engine.can('user-dana', 'update', { type: 'post', id: 'post-123', attributes: { ownerId: 'user-alice' }, }) // -> false ``` The `$` prefix marks a value as a reference into the request rather than a literal. At evaluation time `$subject.id` resolves against the request that is being evaluated. Pass a different owner field with `w.isOwner('resource.attributes.createdBy')`. See [dollar variables](/duck-iam/core/policies/dollar-variables). `eq` is `===`. A subject ID of `'42'` never equals an `ownerId` of `42`. `gt` / `gte` / `lt` / `lte` return `false` unless **both** operands are numbers, so an ISO date string compared with `gte` is always false - use `before` / `after` for temporal values. ## Step 7: multi-tenant scoped roles Assign the same subject different roles per scope, then pass the scope on the check. ```ts // Alice is admin in org-1 but only a viewer in org-2. await engine.admin.assignRole('user-alice', 'admin', 'org-1') await engine.admin.assignRole('user-alice', 'viewer', 'org-2') await engine.can('user-alice', 'manage', { type: 'team', attributes: {} }, undefined, 'org-1') // -> true await engine.can('user-alice', 'manage', { type: 'team', attributes: {} }, undefined, 'org-2') // -> false ``` The engine merges the subject's global roles with the scoped assignments whose scope matches the request. Matching is exact by default (`scopeMode: 'flat'`). Set `scopeMode: 'hierarchical'` on the engine config to treat a dot-delimited scope as a path, so a grant on `'org-1'` applies to `'org-1.team-2.repo-3'`. See [scoped roles](/duck-iam/core/roles/scoped). `engine.getEffectiveRoles(subjectId, scope?)` returns the merged list if you need to see what the engine resolved. ## Step 8: guard a route Every framework wrapper is built on `engine.can()` and takes the same three leading arguments. ### Express ```ts title="src/server.ts" import express from 'express' import { iamAccessMiddleware, iamGuard } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/express' import { engine } from './lib/engine' const app = express() // Option A: global middleware, infers action from the HTTP method and // resource from the first path segment. app.use(iamAccessMiddleware(engine, { getUserId: (req) => req.user?.id ?? null })) // Option B: an explicit per-route guard. app.get('/posts', iamGuard(engine, 'read', 'post'), (req, res) => res.json({ posts: [] })) app.delete('/posts/:id', iamGuard(engine, 'delete', 'post'), (req, res) => res.json({ deleted: true })) app.listen(3000) ``` `iamGuard` reads the resource ID from `req.params.id`. Both helpers reply 401 when `getUserId` returns null and 403 when the engine denies. ### Hono ```ts title="src/worker.ts" import { Hono } from 'hono' import { iamAccessMiddleware, iamGuard } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/hono' import { engine } from './lib/engine' const app = new Hono() app.use('*', iamAccessMiddleware(engine, { getUserId: (c) => (c.get('userId') as string | null) ?? null })) app.delete('/posts/:id', iamGuard(engine, 'delete', 'post'), (c) => c.json({ deleted: true })) export default app ``` ### NestJS ```ts title="src/posts/posts.controller.ts" import { Controller, Delete, Get, Param, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common' import { IamAuthorize, iamNestAccessGuard } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/nest' import { engine } from '../lib/engine' const canActivate = iamNestAccessGuard(engine, { getUserId: (req) => req.user?.sub ?? null }) @Controller('posts') @UseGuards({ canActivate } as never) export class PostsController { @Get() @IamAuthorize({ action: 'read', resource: 'post' }) findAll() { return [] } @Delete(':id') @IamAuthorize({ action: 'delete', resource: 'post' }) remove(@Param('id') id: string) { return { deleted: id } } } ``` `iamNestAccessGuard` returns a `canActivate` body; handlers with no `IamAuthorize` metadata pass through. ### Next.js ```ts title="src/app/api/posts/[id]/route.ts" import { withIamAccess } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/next' import { engine } from '@/lib/engine' import { getSession } from '@/lib/auth' export const DELETE = withIamAccess( engine, 'delete', 'post', async (req, ctx) => { const params = ctx.params instanceof Promise ? await ctx.params : ctx.params return Response.json({ deleted: params?.id }) }, { getUserId: async () => { const session = await getSession() return session?.userId ?? null }, }, ) ``` Since 2.1.0 `withIamAccess` throws at construction when `getUserId` is omitted, and the Hono helpers read only `c.get('userId')` - there is no `x-user-id` header fallback on any framework. A raw request header is spoofable with one `curl`. Derive identity from a cookie session, a JWT your middleware verified, or mTLS. See [production hardening](/duck-iam/guides/production). Per-framework detail: [express](/duck-iam/integrations/server/express), [hono](/duck-iam/integrations/server/hono), [nest](/duck-iam/integrations/server/nest), [next](/duck-iam/integrations/server/next). ## Step 9: send a permission map to the client `engine.permissions()` evaluates a batch of checks in one pass and returns a map keyed by `iamBuildPermissionKey`: `action:resource[:resourceId]`, or `@scope:action:resource[:resourceId]` when a scope is passed - the leading `@` is what keeps a scoped key unambiguous, so it is never dropped. Serialize it into your page and the client checks become synchronous object lookups. ```tsx title="src/app/layout.tsx" import { getIamPermissions } from '@gentleduck/iam/server/next' import { engine } from '@/lib/engine' import { getSession } from '@/lib/auth' import { AccessProvider } from '@/lib/access-client' export default async function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const session = await getSession() const permissions = await getIamPermissions(engine, session.userId, [ { action: 'create', resource: 'post' }, { action: 'delete', resource: 'post' }, { action: 'manage', resource: 'team' }, ]) return {children} } ``` ```ts title="src/lib/access-client.tsx" 'use client' import React from 'react' import { createIamAccessControl } from '@gentleduck/iam/client/react' export const { AccessProvider, useAccess, usePermissions, Can, Cannot } = createIamAccessControl(React) ``` ```tsx title="src/components/post-actions.tsx" 'use client' import { Can, Cannot, useAccess } from '@/lib/access-client' export function PostActions() { const { can } = useAccess() return (
{can('update', 'post') && }

You do not have permission to manage this team.
) } ``` `createIamAccessControl(React)` takes the host React module as an argument so the package never bundles its own copy. `permissions()` refuses batches over 1024 checks - that is a caller bug, and it throws rather than failing closed. See [permission map](/duck-iam/integrations/client/permission-map) and [React client](/duck-iam/integrations/client/react). ## Debugging with explain When a decision surprises you, `engine.explain()` returns the whole trace. It is development-mode only and throws the coded `IAM_ENGINE_EXPLAIN_UNAVAILABLE` otherwise. ```ts const trace = await engine.explain('user-dana', 'delete', { type: 'post', id: 'post-123', attributes: { ownerId: 'user-alice' }, }) trace.decision // AccessControl.IDecision: { allowed, effect, reason, duration, timestamp, ... } trace.summary // human-readable one-liner trace.subject // { id, roles, scopedRolesApplied, attributes } trace.policies // Explain.IPolicyTrace[]: per policy, per rule, per condition, // with actual vs expected for every comparison ``` `explain()` does not fire `afterEvaluate`, `onDeny`, or `onError` - it is read-only. It does run `beforeEvaluate`, because that hook changes what is evaluated. Field-by-field reference: [explain](/duck-iam/advanced/explain). ## Before you ship The engine defaults to `mode: 'development'`, which allocates a full `IDecision` per policy per request. Production deployments should set `mode: 'production'`, call `engine.preload()` at boot, and `engine.dispose()` on shutdown. Work through the [production hardening checklist](/duck-iam/guides/production) before you take traffic. ## See also * [Production hardening](/duck-iam/guides/production) - the pre-flight checklist, with a link per item * [Cookbook](/duck-iam/guides/cookbook) - recipes for the patterns above ownership and tenancy * [Troubleshooting](/duck-iam/guides/troubleshooting) - symptom, cause, fix, keyed to real error messages * [Core concepts](/duck-iam/core) - policies, rules, conditions, combining algorithms * [Pairing with duck-auth](/duck-iam/guides/auth-bridge) - where the subject ID comes from * [Real-world examples](/duck-iam/guides/examples) - this walkthrough's patterns, wired into four real framework backends

content: Self-contained recipes, each checked against the current `@gentleduck/iam` signatures. Swap the actions and resources for yours and ship. Every snippet assumes the typed config and engine from the [quick start](/duck-iam/guides): ```ts title="src/lib/access.ts" import { createIam } from '@gentleduck/iam/core' export const access = createIam({ actions: ['create', 'read', 'update', 'delete', 'export', 'approve', 'manage'] as const, resources: ['post', 'comment', 'user', 'report', 'expense', 'billing'] as const, roles: ['viewer', 'editor', 'admin', 'author', 'auditor'] as const, scopes: ['org-1', 'org-2'] as const, }) ``` Under the default `policyCombine: 'and'` every **applicable** policy must allow. A policy is skipped as NotApplicable when its `targets` do not match **or** when no rule's action/resource shape matches. But once a rule's shape matches and its conditions fail, the policy falls to `defaultEffect` - deny - and vetoes the request even if a role granted it. That is what makes the ownership recipe below work, and it is also the single most common surprise. See [cross-policy combination](/duck-iam/core/cross-policy). ## Picking a combining algorithm Almost every recipe below starts by choosing how the rules inside one policy combine. This is the decision. B{"Is one rule a veto?"} B -- "yes" --> C["deny-overrides"] B -- "no" --> D{"Several ways to qualify?"} D -- "yes" --> E["allow-overrides"] D -- "no" --> F{"Does an override outrank the rest?"} F -- "yes" --> G["highest-priority"] F -- "no" --> H["first-match"] C --> C1["Suspension, MFA gate, embargo"] E --> E1["Public or owner reads"] G --> G1["Break-glass"] H --> H1["Ordered list, first hit wins"]`} /> `deny-overrides` is the default and the right answer whenever a single condition must be able to veto everything else - the suspension, MFA, and embargo recipes all take that branch. `allow-overrides` is for the opposite shape, where any one of several rules qualifying is enough, which is what the public-or-owner read recipe needs. `highest-priority` reads the numeric `priority` on each rule and is what makes break-glass work without reordering the policy. `first-match` returns the first matching rule regardless of effect, so it depends on rule order and is the one to avoid unless that ordering is the point. ## Owners can edit their own resources Two ways. Prefer the role form when ownership is the whole rule; use the policy form when you also need it to veto other grants. ```ts title="Role form" export const author = access .defineRole('author') .grantRead('post', 'comment') .grant('create', 'post') .grantWhen('update', 'post', (w) => w.isOwner()) .grantWhen('delete', 'post', (w) => w.isOwner()) .build() ``` ```ts title="Policy form" export const ownersPolicy = access .definePolicy('owners') .name('Owners only') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .target({ actions: ['update', 'delete'], resources: ['post', 'comment'] }) .rule('owner-writes', (r) => r.allow().on('update', 'delete').of('post', 'comment').when((w) => w.isOwner()), ) .build() ``` `w.isOwner()` emits the condition `resource.attributes.ownerId eq $subject.id`. Pass a different field with `w.isOwner('resource.attributes.createdBy')`. The check must carry the attribute: ```ts await engine.can('user-bob', 'update', { type: 'post', id: 'post-1', attributes: { ownerId: 'user-bob' }, }) // -> true ``` The `.target(...)` on the policy form matters: without it the policy would be applicable to `create post` too, find no matching rule shape - and so stay NotApplicable - but adding the target documents the intent and lets `build()` catch a mismatch as `UNREACHABLE_TARGET`. ## Public and private resources ```ts export const visibilityPolicy = access .definePolicy('visibility') .name('Public and private reads') .algorithm('allow-overrides') .target({ actions: ['read'], resources: ['post'] }) .rule('public-read', (r) => r.allow().on('read').of('post').when((w) => w.resourceAttr('visibility', 'eq', 'public')), ) .rule('owner-read', (r) => r.allow().on('read').of('post').when((w) => w.isOwner()), ) .build() ``` `allow-overrides` means either rule matching is enough. `resourceAttr('visibility', ...)` is shorthand for the dot-path `resource.attributes.visibility`; after `.of('post')` the builder narrows the type so your editor autocompletes that resource's attributes. ## Role hierarchy ```ts export const viewer = access.defineRole('viewer').grantRead('post', 'comment').build() export const editor = access .defineRole('editor') .inherits('viewer') .grant('create', 'post') .grant('update', 'post') .build() export const admin = access .defineRole('admin') .inherits('editor') .grant('delete', 'post') .grant('manage', 'user') .build() ``` `inherits` takes role **IDs**, not role objects, and the parents must exist in the adapter - a dangling parent is caught by `validateRoles()` as `DANGLING_INHERIT`. Inheritance is flattened once at load, not per request, and cycles are cut by a shallowest-depth memo rather than recursing forever. The runtime caps the chain at `MAX_INHERITANCE_DEPTH` (32) and the validator reports `INHERITANCE_TOO_DEEP` past it. See [inheritance](/duck-iam/core/roles/inheritance). Inherited grants cannot be subtracted. To take something back from a parent, add a deny policy. ## One role per organization ```ts await engine.admin.assignRole('user-alice', 'admin', 'org-1') await engine.admin.assignRole('user-alice', 'viewer', 'org-2') await engine.can('user-alice', 'delete', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }, undefined, 'org-1') // -> true await engine.can('user-alice', 'delete', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }, undefined, 'org-2') // -> false ``` When you build the subject yourself instead of letting the engine resolve it, the same thing looks like this: ```ts import type { IamRequest } from '@gentleduck/iam/core' const subject: IamRequest.ISubject = { id: 'user-alice', roles: [], scopedRoles: [ { role: 'admin', scope: 'org-1' }, { role: 'viewer', scope: 'org-2' }, ], attributes: {}, } await engine.authorize({ subject, action: 'delete', resource: { type: 'post', attributes: {} }, scope: 'org-1' }) ``` `scopedRoles` is an array of `{ role, scope?, attributes? }`, not a keyed object. Entries whose `scope` matches the request are merged into the effective role list alongside the subject's global `roles`. `engine.getEffectiveRoles(subjectId, scope)` returns that merged list. See [scoped roles](/duck-iam/core/roles/scoped). ## Hierarchical scopes For GitHub- or Slack-shaped tenancy where a grant at the org level should apply to every team and repository below it: ```ts const engine = access.createEngine({ adapter, scopeMode: 'hierarchical', scopeCombine: 'union', }) await engine.admin.assignRole('user-alice', 'admin', 'org-1') await engine.can('user-alice', 'delete', { type: 'post', attributes: {} }, undefined, 'org-1.team-2.repo-3') // -> true: the org-1 grant covers every descendant scope ``` `scopeMode: 'hierarchical'` treats a dot-delimited scope as a path and matches a grant at any ancestor level. `scopeCombine: 'union'` (default) ORs in every matching level; `'override'` keeps only the most specific match, so a narrower grant shadows a broader one instead of adding to it. A scope with no dots degrades to exact match, so enabling it is safe for apps that never use dotted scopes. ## Time-bound access Two flavours. Numeric comparisons on an environment value: ```ts export const businessHours = access .definePolicy('business-hours') .name('Business hours only') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .target({ actions: ['export'], resources: ['report'] }) .rule('deny-out-of-hours', (r) => r.deny().on('export').of('report').whenAny((w) => w.env('hour', 'lt', 9).env('hour', 'gte', 18)), ) .rule('allow-in-hours', (r) => r.allow().on('export').of('report')) .build() await engine.can('user-bob', 'export', { type: 'report', attributes: {} }, { hour: new Date().getUTCHours() }) ``` Temporal comparisons against the evaluation clock: ```ts export const embargo = access .definePolicy('embargo') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .target({ actions: ['read'], resources: ['report'] }) .rule('deny-before-publish', (r) => r .deny() .on('read') .of('report') .when((w) => w.check('environment.now', 'before', '$resource.attributes.publishAt')), ) .rule('allow-after-publish', (r) => r.allow().on('read').of('report')) .build() ``` `environment.now` is stamped by the engine as `Date.now()` on every request unless a `beforeEvaluate` hook already pinned it - which is how you get a deterministic clock in tests. The `before` and `after` operators coerce both operands to epoch milliseconds (numbers pass through, ISO-8601 strings are parsed) and return `false` when either side is not temporal. `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, and `lte` return `false` unless **both** operands are numbers. An ISO-8601 timestamp compared with `gte` is always false, which reads as a working deny rule and a broken allow rule. Use `before` / `after` for anything temporal. See [condition operators](/duck-iam/core/policies/conditions). ## Require MFA for high-risk actions With the [duck-auth bridge](/duck-iam/guides/auth-bridge), the subject carries the session's assurance level as a number. ```ts export const mfaPolicy = access .definePolicy('mfa-required') .name('AAL2 for destructive actions') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .target({ actions: ['delete', 'export'], resources: ['user', 'billing'] }) .rule('deny-below-aal2', (r) => r.deny().on('delete', 'export').of('user', 'billing').when((w) => w.attr('aal', 'lt', 2)), ) .rule('allow-at-aal2', (r) => r.allow().on('delete', 'export').of('user', 'billing')) .build() ``` `deny-overrides` makes the deny rule win whenever it matches, regardless of rule order. The allow rule is the catch-all for sessions that clear the bar. `w.attr('aal', ...)` prefixes `subject.attributes.` for you. ## Field-level permissions Pass the changed field list on the request environment and test it with set operators. ```ts export const fieldsPolicy = access .definePolicy('billing-fields') .name('Billing fields are admin-only') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .target({ actions: ['update'], resources: ['user'] }) .rule('deny-billing-fields', (r) => r .deny() .on('update') .of('user') .when((w) => w .check('environment.fieldsChanged', 'contains', 'billing.cardNumber') .not((n) => n.contains('subject.roles', 'admin')), ), ) .rule('allow-update', (r) => r.allow().on('update').of('user')) .build() ``` That deny fires only when a non-admin touches a billing field. `contains` on an array is membership; stacking two conditions inside one `.when()` is AND; `.not()` negates the group inside it, which is what turns "is an admin" into "is not an admin". Drop the `.not()` and the rule denies admins and nobody else. ```ts await engine.can('user-bob', 'update', { type: 'user', id: 'user-9', attributes: {} }, { fieldsChanged: ['billing.address'], }) ``` `subset_of` and `superset_of` are the operators for whole-set comparisons: `w.check('environment.fieldsChanged', 'subset_of', ['title', 'body'])` allows a write only when every changed field is in the safe list. ## Deny a suspended subject regardless of role A cross-cutting veto. Under the default `policyCombine: 'and'`, one deny is final. ```ts export const suspensionPolicy = access .definePolicy('suspension') .name('Suspended subjects cannot write') .algorithm('deny-overrides') .target({ actions: ['create', 'update', 'delete'] }) .rule('deny-suspended', (r) => r .deny() .on('create', 'update', 'delete') .of('*') .when((w) => w.attr('status', 'eq', 'suspended')), ) .rule('allow-otherwise', (r) => r.allow().on('create', 'update', 'delete').of('*')) .build() await engine.admin.setAttributes('user-bob', { status: 'suspended' }) await engine.cache.invalidateSubject('user-bob') ``` `setAttributes` merges into the subject's attribute bag and invalidates that subject's cache entry itself, so the explicit `invalidateSubject` is only needed if you wrote through the adapter directly. Keys are built by `iamBuildPermissionKey(action, resource, resourceId?, scope?)` as `action:resource[:resourceId]`, or `@scope:action:resource[:resourceId]` when a scope is passed - the leading `@` is what keeps a scoped key unambiguous, so it is never dropped - with `:` and `\` backslash-escaped per segment - do not build the key by hand. See [PermissionMap reference](/duck-iam/integrations/client/permission-map) for the full escaping rules. Batches over 1024 checks throw. See [validation](/duck-iam/advanced/validation). ## See also * [Quick start](/duck-iam/guides) - the config, roles, and engine these recipes assume * [Pairing with duck-auth](/duck-iam/guides/auth-bridge) - where `subject.attributes.aal` comes from * [Production hardening](/duck-iam/guides/production) - before any of this takes real traffic * [Troubleshooting](/duck-iam/guides/troubleshooting) - when a recipe does not behave * [Combining algorithms](/duck-iam/core/policies/combining-algorithms) - `deny-overrides` vs `allow-overrides` vs `first-match` vs `highest-priority`

Pass `{ telemetry: false }` as the fourth argument to skip per-check `onMetrics` on hot UI gates, worth roughly 2x throughput. `access.checks([...])` is a typed pass-through: it constrains the tuples to your declared actions, resources, and scopes without changing the value. ## Shadow-test a new policy before enabling it Run a second engine over the same adapter data plus the candidate policy, compare, and log the disagreements. ```ts import { IamMemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/iam/adapters/memory' const shadowAdapter = new IamMemoryAdapter({ roles: allRoles, policies: [...currentPolicies, candidatePolicy], }) const shadowEngine = access.createEngine({ adapter: shadowAdapter }) app.post('/api/posts/:id', async (req, res) => { const args = ['user-bob', 'update', { type: 'post', id: req.params.id, attributes: {} }] as const const real = await engine.can(...args) const shadow = await shadowEngine.can(...args) if (real !== shadow) { log.warn({ event: 'iam-shadow-mismatch', subject: args[0], action: args[1], real, shadow }) } if (!real) return res.status(403).end() // ... }) ``` Both engines must run the same `policyCombine` and `defaultEffect` or the comparison is meaningless. Promote the candidate with `engine.admin.savePolicy(candidatePolicy)` once the mismatch rate is zero for a full traffic cycle - or ship it through [`admin.export()` / `import()`](/duck-iam/guides/production#snapshot-policies-and-roles-environment-promotion) as part of the normal promotion path. ## Validate the whole catalog at boot ```ts const roleResult = access.validateRoles(allRoles) if (!roleResult.valid) { for (const issue of roleResult.issues) { console.error(`[iam] ${issue.type} ${issue.code}${issue.roleId ? ` role={issue.message}`) } throw new Error('iam role catalog is invalid') } for (const policy of currentPolicies) { const result = access.validatePolicy(policy) if (!result.valid) throw new Error(`policy {result.issues.map((i) => i.code).join(', ')}`) } ``` `IamValidate.IResult` is `{ valid, issues }`, and `valid` is false only when an `error`-type issue exists - warnings such as `BROAD_ALLOW` do not flip it. Both builders already validate on `build()`; running the catalog check at boot catches rows that arrived from an adapter rather than from a builder. See [validation](/duck-iam/advanced/validation). ## See also * [Quick start](/duck-iam/guides) - the config, roles, and engine these recipes assume * [Pairing with duck-auth](/duck-iam/guides/auth-bridge) - where `subject.attributes.aal` comes from * [Production hardening](/duck-iam/guides/production) - before any of this takes real traffic * [Troubleshooting](/duck-iam/guides/troubleshooting) - when a recipe does not behave * [Combining algorithms](/duck-iam/core/policies/combining-algorithms) - `deny-overrides` vs `allow-overrides` vs `first-match` vs `highest-priority`
